title: Should I make voluntary lump-sum overpayments on my Plan 2 student loan earning £68,000?
question: I currently earn £68,000 in London with a remaining Plan 2 student loan balance of around £44,000. My parents suggested I pay it off early to avoid the 7%+ interest accumulation. Is this mathematically sound, or am I better off investing into a Stocks & Shares ISA?
answer:
Great question Oliver. On Plan 2 at £68,000 salary, your mandatory repayment is 9% of income above £27,295 (£3,663/year). Because of interest (RPI + up to 3%), your £44k debt is growing by ~£3,000+ each year in interest alone! At this repayment rate, you will likely pay on the loan for nearly 20+ years before it clears, meaning a voluntary overpayment DOES save you real money IF your career progression stays at or above £68k.

However, before overpaying, consider two critical factors:
1. Cash liquidity: once you pay SLC, you cannot borrow that money back for a home deposit.
2. Expected market returns: a global equity index ISA has historically returned 7-9% nominal compound growth with full tax-free liquidity.

title: How do you handle API rate limits and token costs when building CV parser agents?
question: I'm developing an AI resume scanner using Gemini Flash, but when batch processing or when users test frequently, token costs and rate limits become a concern. How did you optimize UK JobMatch AI?
answer:
Hi Priya! In UK JobMatch AI, I implemented a two-stage hybrid filter:

1. Stage 1 uses purely local Python text processing (regex, keyword frequency, title matching, and TF-IDF style scoring) to eliminate 80% of irrelevant job postings before touching any LLM.
2. Stage 2 only sends the top candidate matches (e.g. top 5-10 jobs) to Google Gemini Flash.

Furthermore, we extract skills once and cache the structured JSON representation of the CV, rather than passing raw multi-page text repeatedly. This dropped our token usage by 85% and easily keeps the app within Google AI Studio's free tier limits!

title: Maximizing higher-rate pension tax relief with a variable bonus
question: My base salary is £55k, but I receive a discretionary year-end bonus of ~£20k taking me to £75k. How should I approach salary sacrifice into a SIPP vs workplace pension?
answer:
Hello David. If your employer offers salary sacrifice (Bonus Sacrifice), that is almost always superior to a personal SIPP contribution because you save both the 40% higher rate Income Tax AND 2% employee National Insurance (plus your employer may also pass on part of their 13.8%/15% employer NI savings into your pension pot!).

If salary sacrifice isn't available, contributing into a personal SIPP gives you 20% basic tax relief credited automatically, and you claim the remaining 20% back via your Self Assessment tax return or HMRC PAYE tax code adjustment.
